title: Standardizing instructional design standards on Mac: how to fix inconsistent team workflows
metaTitle: Standardizing Instructional Design Standards: A Guide for Mac Users
description: Learn how to establish instructional design standards on your Mac, reduce project redesigns, and improve team consistency without buying expensive software.
intro: Standardizing instructional design standards ensures your team delivers consistent learning experiences while reducing the time spent on repetitive tasks. Many instructional designers struggle because they treat design as a rigid, linear process rather than a dynamic, iterative one.
tldr: Standardization prevents costly redesigns by catching constraints early in the discovery phase.
Use flexible frameworks like ADDIE or SAM to adapt to project realities.
Centralize your workflow with shared templates and common language.
Prioritize discovery to align stakeholder assumptions with measurable performance goals.

blocks.text: Why standardizing instructional design standards is hard

The primary issue is the myth that instructional design is a perfectly linear path. Academic models often paint a picture of a clean, step by step progression. In reality, you are negotiating with stakeholders, juggling shifting budgets, and managing technical limitations simultaneously. When you ignore these constraints, you end up with project delays and expensive rework.
Common costs of inconsistent design workflows

Inconsistency is expensive. When you do not have a standardized process, you often start from zero on every new course. This leads to efficiency losses and burnout. You waste time recreating basic assets and structures that should be readily available in a template library.
Practical steps to fix your design process

items: Adopt flexible frameworks: Use ADDIE or SAM as a guide, not a rigid law.
Prioritize discovery: Conduct a needs assessment before you open any authoring tool.
Create a shared language: Ensure everyone on the team defines key terms the same way.
Filter by need: Only include content that directly supports the learning objectives.

blocks.text: Tools for instructional design on Mac

Instructional designers on Mac often rely on a mix of tools to maintain consistency. Miro is excellent for mapping out course flows before you build. Canva helps you keep visual assets uniform. Cognota can help manage your operations if your team is large enough to require centralized project tracking.

Lazur helps you maintain your standards by acting as a quick reference for your team's guidelines. When you are deep in a project, you can ask Lazur to recall your specific formatting rules or check if a file follows your established naming convention. It keeps your focus on the design work instead of digging through folders.

faq.question: Why is it hard to standardize instructional design?
faq.answer: It is hard because projects are dynamic. Rigid models do not account for the constant changes in stakeholder needs and project constraints.

faq.question: What is the biggest cost of not having standards?
faq.answer: The biggest cost is time lost to rework. When you do not have a standard process, you end up redesigning assets that could have been templated.

causes.title: The Linear Myth
causes.text: Treating design as a rigid, unchangeable process ignores the reality of project constraints.

causes.title: Stakeholder Misalignment
causes.text: Starting projects with untested assumptions rather than a clear discovery phase leads to confusion.

fixes.title: Flexible Frameworks
fixes.text: Use models like ADDIE or SAM as adaptable guides rather than strict rules.

fixes.title: Need-to-Know Filtering
fixes.text: Keep training focused by strictly separating essential content from nice-to-have information.
